content.text:
**I would hold #144, #149, #150, #153, and #155 for corrections.** #145, #151, and #152 look stronger; I found no confirmed blocking defect in their reviewed implementation, though verification gaps remain.

I reviewed the eight current heads, examined relevant callers and tests, checked CI failures, and ran focused reproductions. All heads remained unchanged during the review. Your working files were untouched.

| PR / reviewed head | Code quality | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| [#144 — Field builders](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/144) · `090dbf4` | **Good API work; inconsistent runtime integration.** Strong type coverage, but scope expanded into query and mutation semantics. | Fix query inconsistency |
| [#145 — Ancestor inactivity](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/145) · `d831914` | **Good.** Centralized ownership rules, enforcement across write paths, meaningful migration and concurrency tests. | Strongest candidate; checks green |
| [#149 — Client profiles](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/149) · `44dc18b` | **Mixed.** Sensible trusted-identity boundary, but the testing/reporting code can provide misleading evidence. | Fix correctness and typecheck |
| [#150 — Transport-neutral testing](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/150) · `e0cd125` | **Mixed.** Useful transport abstractions; failure cleanup and diagnostic fidelity need work. | Fix failure paths |
| [#151 — Namespace storage](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/151) · `2e3f1f1` | **Good, well scoped.** Clear logical/physical separation and explicit completeness checks. | Still draft; PostgreSQL integration evidence needed |
| [#152 — Placement auth context](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/152) · `a2685f2` | **Good security structure; substantial maintenance burden.** Extensive lifecycle coverage, but considerable duplicated TS/Python logic and custom URL handling. | No confirmed blocker; resolve red checks |
| [#153 — Resource selectors](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/153) · `4eb55d0` | **Readable, but incomplete contract integration.** Tests cover the new parser more thoroughly than actual client request shapes. | Fix authorization example and sync compatibility |
| [#155 — Create presets](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/155) · `6886076` | **Prototype quality.** Codec/compiler separation is useful, but project application does not meet its safety promise. | Highest concern: user-file loss |

**#155: unsafe project application**

- **P1 — Existing unmanaged files are overwritten.** `applyPreset()` accepts an existing directory without preset state, then treats missing ownership hashes as permission to update files. My reproduction replaced an existing `package.json` and removed its custom script while returning success. Existing `App.tsx`, configuration, and README files face the same path. Require explicit ownership or a conflict before replacing them. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/6886076a5c34a766a249aa439041752d1a92b133/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L177)
- **P1 — Partial apply removes protection for other files.** The new state contains hashes only for files included in that partial operation. I reproduced: initialize → edit `App.tsx` → apply font only → full apply. The final apply silently destroyed the edit. Preserve untouched files’ ownership hashes. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/6886076a5c34a766a249aa439041752d1a92b133/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L133)
- **P2 — `--only font` also changes theme settings.** Both partial domains regenerate the entire theme stylesheet from the incoming preset, including colors, radius, and density. Merge only the selected domain into the existing preset. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/6886076a5c34a766a249aa439041752d1a92b133/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L135)
- **Build blocker — Missing lockfile update.** CI’s `npm ci` fails because `@uifn/create@0.0.1` is missing from the lockfile. This is directly attributable to the new workspace. [CI log](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/actions/runs/33836053237/job/100909081069)

**#153: authorization and protocol mismatches**

- **P1 — The recommended authorization callback permits broad requests.** `selectors.every(...)` returns true for `[]`. An authenticated caller therefore passes this resource allowlist for unrestricted search, clone, or global pull—even with no allowed resources. I reproduced the unrestricted-search decision. Handle broad and resource-less operations explicitly; the warning below the example does not make the example safe. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/docs/content/docs/documentation/security/resource-selectors.mdx#L87)
- **P1 — Normal sync requests acquire a bogus resource selector.** Pull extraction includes `__datafn_actor_feed__`. The standard sync client sends that cursor, while the server explicitly excludes it from resource enumeration. The new allowlist integration consequently rejects legitimate sync requests. Reproduced. [Extractor](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/core/src/protocol.ts#L439), [client](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/client/src/sync/engine.ts#L689)
- **P2 — Batch requests bypass explicit version validation.** A batch containing `{resource:"todos", protocolVersion:"2"}` succeeds and is stamped version `"1"`. Reproduced. Validate batch version metadata consistently with single requests. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/core/src/protocol.ts#L550)

**#149: unreliable compatibility evidence**

- **P2 — Reports silently lose entries after 32.** Redaction slices every array, including results, checks, and tool names, before the report-size mechanism runs. A 40-result probe retained only 32 while preserving `status:"complete"` and `droppedResults:0`. Separate redaction from explicitly reported truncation. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/44dc18b94c3f8b671a6956e9ad9a4ca61bb6cc01/mcpfn/core/src/client-profile.ts#L583)
- **P2 — `handlerReached:false` does not verify handler execution.** It merely checks `isError`. A handler can execute, perform side effects, and return an error while the assertion passes. My probe confirmed this false positive. Instrument handler invocation or narrow the assertion’s promise. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/44dc18b94c3f8b671a6956e9ad9a4ca61bb6cc01/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profiles.ts#L408)
- **P2 — Portability analysis misses nested schema locations.** The walker skips locations such as `additionalProperties` and `$defs`. A remote `$ref` under `additionalProperties` produced no finding despite the default remote-reference rejection policy. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/44dc18b94c3f8b671a6956e9ad9a4ca61bb6cc01/mcpfn/core/src/client-profile.ts#L699)
- **Build blocker — New reporting code fails typecheck.** The release gate reports TS2352 at `client-profiles.ts:449`, in the new report-redaction cast. This is a concrete failure in changed code. [CI log](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/actions/runs/33834964811/job/100905517059)

**#150: cleanup and test fidelity**

- **P2 — Failed connections leave issued credentials active.** If initialization rejects, no cleanup handle is returned and neither disposal nor revocation runs. My mocked failure recorded one issued credential and zero cleanup calls. The successful connection’s cleanup also skips revocation if an earlier cleanup step throws. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/e0cd1257f74386abee32993452321a0f2d44b325/mcpfn/testing/src/remote-target.ts#L82)
- **P2 — Client-ID mismatch fixtures cannot represent the mismatch.** Registration and authorization-request IDs collapse into one value. Supplying `"registered"` and `"unknown"` produced `"registered"` for both. This can make negative authentication coverage misleading. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/e0cd1257f74386abee32993452321a0f2d44b325/mcpfn/testing/src/host-authorization.ts#L112)
- **P2 — Reporting discards error provenance before classifying it.** Reconstructing a plain `Error` loses its original phase/code. A token-exchange failure classified as `authorization-server` became `mcp-initialization` in the report. Preserve structured provenance through serialization. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/e0cd1257f74386abee32993452321a0f2d44b325/mcpfn/testing/src/reports.ts#L35)

**#144: query results depend on execution path**

- **P2 — Equivalent filters return different records after null normalization.** For a persisted optional, non-nullable field holding `null`, `{label:{eq:null}}` uses the indexed path and returns the row; `{$and:[{label:{eq:null}}]}` normalizes before evaluating and returns nothing. I reproduced both through the changed offline executor. Normalize consistently before both index filtering and scan filtering. [Source](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/090dbf4b84c98bd47c49db8a2b60fcf774955461/datafn/client/src/offline/query.ts#L193)

**Verification limits:** These were focused source-level reproductions, with mocked dependencies where appropriate—not full checkout test-suite runs. #144 and #152’s JavaScript failures occur in unchanged UIFN React tests, so I did not attribute those failures to their changes. #150 and #151 have failed Sonar checks; those failures remain unresolved. For #151, the added tests use synthetic catalogs and memory adapters, leaving real PostgreSQL behavior unproven here. “No confirmed blocker” for #145/#151/#152 is therefore not a merge approval.

I verified #155 still has the reviewed head, `6886076`.

|---|---|---|---|

The decisive weakness in **#155** is its implementation of “safe application.” The reviewed code can overwrite unmanaged project files, discard ownership hashes during partial application, and change unselected settings during theme/font-only operations. These are substantially more consequential than the cloud sessions’ codec defects.

The cloud implementations also introduce incompatible contracts: **A and B use the same `uifn1_` prefix but reject each other’s presets.** Their raw `.uifn/preset.json` format also differs from #155’s state envelope containing the preset and ownership hashes. They cannot be integrated unchanged.

**My recommendation is to improve #155 rather than replace it with either cloud session.** Retain its broader architecture, fix file ownership and partial-update semantics first, and adopt B’s strict canonical-decoding approach with appropriate tests. A offers useful target configuration ideas, but neither cloud session demonstrates a better complete solution.

That recommendation concerns the implementation direction; **none of the three is ready to merge as completed UIF-2**. The comparison uses the earlier focused reproductions and current source verification, not a fresh full-suite run.

**#163 is the best implementation of the four and a meaningful improvement over #155—but it still needs fixes before merging.** Reviewed head: `75018c0`.

| Area | PR #163 | PR #155 | Cloud A / B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature completeness | Broad Create, compiler, CLI, project workflows | Similar broad scope | Preset foundations only |
| Existing-project handling | Merges dependencies and preserves entry points, scripts, README | Could replace consumer files with scaffold files | Not implemented |
| Partial application | Preserves prior ownership hashes and unselected preset fields | Lost hashes and changed unselected settings | Not implemented |
| Styling integration | Uses public component stylesheet and part attributes | More locally defined fixture styling | No Create UI |
| Tests | Adds existing-project preservation/rejection coverage | Missed those scenarios | Narrow codec/CLI coverage |
| Overall | **Preferred foundation; remaining safety defects** | Superseded in quality by #163 | Incomplete alternatives |

The remaining findings that matter most:

1. **P1 — An existing unmanaged theme file can still be overwritten.**  
   On first application, a differing `src/uifn-theme.css` has no recorded ownership hash, so it passes the conflict check. My exact-source probe confirmed a successful plan scheduling it as an update. This is the remaining form of #155’s destructive-write problem. [Conflict check](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/75018c0db87b5b237eb375e78764a2ff3b2b67e1/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L212)

2. **P2 — Legitimate manifest edits can block subsequent application.**  
   #163 merges `package.json`, but then tracks the entire file as generator-owned. I reproduced: apply → add a consumer script → select another icon library → application fails with `UIFN_REGISTRY_DIRTY_CONFLICT` on `package.json`. Manifest ownership needs to cover only the dependency entries the preset manages. [State serialization](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/75018c0db87b5b237eb375e78764a2ff3b2b67e1/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L278)

3. **P2 — Source-mode initialization dry-runs omit actual installation work.**  
   For a nonexistent destination, the function returns before invoking the registry planner. The preview excludes component files and registry metadata and skips the corresponding validation. This is confirmed by the control flow, rather than a runtime reproduction. [Early return](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/75018c0db87b5b237eb375e78764a2ff3b2b67e1/uifn/registry/src/preset/project.ts#L259)

CI provides better evidence than #155: **the 9 preset workflow tests, 7 preset tests, and 3 editor tests passed**. The JavaScript job failed in `@uifn/components-react` tests, not those new suites. Other failing checks still prevent calling the overall result green. [CI run](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/actions/runs/34221990411)

**Recommendation: continue with #163.** It addresses major defects in #155 while retaining its broader implementation. Fix the remaining ownership and dry-run issues, then add lifecycle regression tests. The cloud sessions offer little reason to replace this direction.

Verification was read-only source comparison, CI-log inspection, and focused package-mode probes—not a complete local build or browser acceptance test.

content.text:
**PR #164 is well scoped and readable, but its advertised gateway integration has two concrete gaps.** I would fix those before merging. Reviewed head: `8da10bf`.

1. **P2 — Bodyless status requests are rejected.**  
   `GET /datafn/status` reaches authorization with `payload: null`, but the extractor requires an object. I reproduced `DFQL_INVALID` for that actual request shape. The test uses `{}`, masking the mismatch. [Status handling](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/8da10bf3f3d205e33331b9283251c0fed9f7b5ca/datafn/server/src/resource-selectors.ts#L208)

2. **P2 — REST routes cannot be resolved from this envelope.**  
   REST authorization runs before handlers derive the resource from the URL. GET requests supply no body, and write bodies need not contain `resource`. The new envelope carries only action and payload, so it cannot identify the matched resource. I reproduced rejection of both shapes. Add trusted route parameters or normalize REST requests before extraction. [Envelope contract](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/8da10bf3f3d205e33331b9283251c0fed9f7b5ca/datafn/server/src/resource-selectors.ts#L27)

There is also a smaller defensive-programming issue: a `null` envelope throws native `TypeError` instead of the documented structured error. This requires violating the TypeScript input contract, so I consider it lower priority.

| Quality dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Scope and maintainability | **Good:** four files, straightforward helpers, explicit action handling |
| API design | **Good foundation:** stable errors, schema validation, ordered deduplication, immutable results |
| Protocol integration | **Incomplete:** tests miss actual status and REST authorization inputs |
| Testing | **Good unit coverage:** 24 selector tests passed; CI reports 95 server test files passed |
| Merge readiness | **Fix the integration gaps first** |

One important contract limitation: these are **explicit structural selectors**, not a complete inventory of resources execution may touch. Relation traversal can reach schema-derived targets that this parser deliberately excludes. Documentation should make clear that the result does not replace relation/record authorization.

I also checked the empty-search-list concern: the execution paths inspected return no results for `resources: []`, so I’m **not reporting it as an authorization bypass**.

Overall, this is a solid, focused implementation whose integration claims exceed its coverage. Verification included exact-source probes, route/executor inspection, and CI logs; no code was changed.

| Architecture | Core-owned parser, typed request variants, separate selector collector; server re-exports | Smaller server-owned extractor with a direct action switch |
| Schema validation | Extracts names without checking resource existence | Rejects resources absent from the supplied schema |
| Structural coverage | Broader: search map keys, clone pagination, pull cursors | Simpler: explicit resource lists and schema-wide defaults |
| Broad requests | Can return `[]` despite operation accessing multiple resources | Expands omitted search/clone lists and pull to the schema |
| Bodyless status | Supported | Incorrectly rejected |
| REST wrappers | No path-resource normalization | Same gap |
| Testing | Broader parser tests plus an actual authorization-hook test | Focused unit tests; actual route-shape gaps remain |
| Maintainability | More machinery, but clearer separation and shared action inventory | Easier to follow, but duplicates protocol knowledge in the server |

The most consequential difference is **how they handle requests without explicit resource lists**.

In #153, the documented `selectors.every(...)` authorization example accepts an empty selector list. A broad search, clone, or pull can therefore pass that example without checking every affected resource. #164’s schema expansion avoids that particular failure. [#153 authorization example](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/docs/content/docs/documentation/security/resource-selectors.mdx#L87)

#153 also retains two previously confirmed problems:

- It treats the reserved `__datafn_actor_feed__` cursor as an application resource, potentially rejecting normal sync requests.
- Batch parsing bypasses explicit protocol-version validation.

#164 avoids those particular mechanisms, but has its own integration defects: bodyless status requests fail, and REST requests cannot supply their URL-derived resource through its envelope. Its external envelope version is also a different contract from #153’s payload protocol version—not a drop-in equivalent.

**My recommendation:** use #164’s schema validation and broad-request handling, while adopting #153’s core-owned parser, shared action inventory, and integration-testing approach. Preserve the distinction between *explicit structural selectors* and *all resources execution may touch*; neither implementation should replace relation or record authorization.

For the immediate choice, **I prefer #164 after fixing status and REST support**. #153’s broader implementation does not outweigh its more consequential authorization-example and sync defects.

**Considering DATA-6 and its supporting architecture plan, I revise my recommendation: #153 is the better foundation.** My earlier preference for #164 weighted schema-based authorization behavior more heavily than the issue’s central requirement: a canonical, parser-aligned structural contract.

The plan explicitly prefers **parsing into a versioned, discriminated protocol envelope, then extracting selectors through an exhaustive visitor**. #153 follows that design much more closely. [Architecture & Delivery Plan](https://linear.app/21n/document/data-6-architecture-and-delivery-plan-8556ea15ae1f)

| DATA-6 requirement | #153 | #164 |
|---|---|---|
| Typed parsed-request representation | Discriminated protocol union | Returns action and selectors; no operation representation |
| Separate exhaustive selector visitor | Implemented | Extraction happens inside its own parser |
| Prevent protocol drift | Shared action inventory, exhaustive visitor, integration test | Independent action union and switch; weaker connection to server parsing |
| Structural selector coverage | Includes protocol map keys and pagination selectors | Omits several positions; substitutes schema-wide defaults |
| Ignore application data | Implemented | Implemented |
| Gateway integration evidence | Actual authorization-hook test | Unit tests only |
| Unsupported-version handling | Present, with the batch validation defect | Validates its external envelope version |

Two corrections to my earlier assessment:

- **Returning every schema resource is not automatically more correct.** DATA-6 requests structural selectors and leaves selector-less-operation semantics as an explicit design decision. #164’s expansion needs justification under that contract.
- **Discovering every indirectly accessed relation target is not an acceptance requirement.** The plan explicitly preserves the structural boundary and calls for explicit protocol variants for future indirect addressing. I would not block either PR merely for excluding execution-derived relation targets.

**#153 still needs fixes:** the unsafe empty-list authorization example, reserved actor-feed cursor handling, and batch version validation remain valid findings. It also needs stronger evidence that its new protocol model stays aligned with actual execution parsing—sharing an action inventory alone does not establish that.

Neither review established the required downstream Skillplane test with its local traversal removed. That remains a completion gap. [DATA-6 requirements](https://linear.app/21n/issue/DATA-6/expose-canonical-structural-resource-selector-extraction)

**Recommendation: finish #153 against the acceptance criteria.** Borrow useful validation and immutable-result practices from #164, but retain #153’s parser/visitor architecture. #164 is a concise helper; #153 is closer to the canonical protocol capability the issue asks for.

why #153 is better than #164 when you read the issue? explain me the problem and 2 solutions and the difference in simplest terms

The problem is: **a gateway needs to know which resource a request targets, without mistaking ordinary user data for an instruction.**

For example:

```json
{
  "resource": "tasks",
  "record": {
    "resource": "secret-documents"
  }
}
```

This request targets **tasks**. `"secret-documents"` is just a value being saved. Searching the entire JSON for fields named `resource` would give the wrong answer.

DATA-6 also wants this distinction to keep working automatically as DataFn adds new request formats.

**#153’s approach: understand the request first, then extract its targets.**

It creates a typed representation of the request—query, mutation, transaction, and so on. A separate extractor reads that representation.

Think of it as: **read a form using its official structure, then collect the resource fields.**

When another request type is added to that shared representation, TypeScript can flag that the extractor needs updating. This is the architecture the issue asks for. #153 still needs stronger integration with actual server parsing to fully deliver that promise.

**#164’s approach: inspect the incoming request using a separate set of rules.**

It says: “For a query, read `resource`; for a transaction, inspect `steps`; for search, inspect `resources`.” It also checks names against the application’s resource list.

Think of it as: **keep a checklist describing where resource fields usually appear.**

That is simpler and useful today. But when the server accepts a new request format, this separate checklist can become outdated. Checking that resource names exist does not prevent that drift.

| | #153 | #164 |
|---|---|---|
| Main strength | Structure designed to evolve with the protocol | Small, straightforward implementation |
| Main weakness | More complex; shared-parser integration still incomplete | Separate parsing rules can drift |
| Fit for DATA-6 | Closer to the requested long-term solution | Useful helper, weaker architectural fit |

**Why my recommendation changed:** I initially focused on today’s behavior, where #164 has some safer defaults. Reading the issue showed that its central goal is also **preventing future disagreement between the server and the extractor**. #153 is better positioned to solve that.

That makes #153 the better **foundation**, not the more bug-free PR or one ready to merge.
give me in a question format that I can ask the agent which created the PR 164 on why it chose that approach despite the issue documents
UIF-2?
dude - give me descriptive question that I can ask

For DATA-6, the issue and Architecture & Delivery Plan call for a versioned, discriminated protocol representation followed by an exhaustive selector visitor, with shared parser/extractor tests to prevent request-shape drift.

PR #164 instead introduces a separate action switch that reads raw payloads and validates resource names against the application schema. Why did you choose this approach over the documented architecture? Was it a deliberate tradeoff, or was there a limitation in DataFn’s existing parser that prevented reuse?

Please explain how this implementation ensures that newly supported request shapes cannot be accepted by the server but missed by the extractor. Also, how do schema-wide expansion for omitted selectors and the lack of a reusable parsed-request representation fit the intended structural-only contract? If the current approach does not provide the guarantees required by DATA-6, what changes would you make to align it with the issue and supporting documents?

this is what it responded:





It was an expedient tradeoff, but it was the wrong tradeoff for DATA-6.

DataFn currently has no single canonical request parser. Validation is fragmented across route handlers:

- Query and mutation use dedicated validators.
- Transactions contain their own wrapped/bare-step discrimination.
- Push, clone, reconcile, and search validate their envelopes independently.
- Several sync routes defer parts of validation to execution functions.

I treated that fragmentation as a reason to add an endpoint-aware structural parser beside the routes. That produced a useful safety improvement over recursive traversal, but it did not satisfy the documented architecture. Nothing fundamentally prevented reuse; proper reuse required refactoring those route validators into a shared, versioned parser first, which I avoided to limit the change’s size.

That caused three architectural problems in PR #164:

- `action + unknown payload` is not a discriminated parsed protocol representation.
- The extractor duplicates protocol-shape knowledge in its own switch, so parser/extractor drift remains possible.
- Application-schema validation is mixed into selector extraction, even though the visitor should operate on already parsed protocol selectors. Schema validation belongs in the parsing/validation stage.

The intended implementation should instead:

1. Define a versioned discriminated union for every supported protocol envelope.
2. Make HTTP routes and transport-neutral execution parse through that representation.
3. Implement selector extraction as an exhaustive visitor over the parsed union.
4. Test each fixture through both parsing and extraction, so adding a protocol variant fails compilation or conformance tests until the visitor handles it.
5. Keep selector extraction structural; application schema checks can happen during parsing but should not be the visitor’s responsibility.

So: there was a real limitation in the existing parser architecture, but it did not justify deviating from the plan. I should have surfaced the required parser refactor and implemented it rather than silently substituting a parallel raw-payload switch.

The agent’s response is largely correct and explains the tradeoff clearly: **it reduced the PR’s scope by introducing a second place that understands request formats, while DATA-6 specifically aims to prevent those interpretations from drifting apart.**

One qualification matters: **#153 also does not fully solve that problem yet.** It introduces the intended parsed union and visitor, but we haven’t established that the server’s execution routes consume that same representation. A better-shaped parallel parser can still drift.

I also wouldn’t automatically require rewriting every route validator. The issue allows a parsed representation **or shared versioned schemas**. The essential guarantee is that execution and extraction agree on accepted request structure; existing operation-specific validation can remain.

You could reply:

> Thanks—that explains the mismatch. Please propose the smallest change that makes request-shape interpretation shared between server execution and selector extraction, rather than introducing another parallel parser. Identify which existing validators can remain, which structural parsing must become shared, and how conformance tests will prove both paths interpret the same request identically. Also assess whether PR #153 provides a reusable foundation, while explicitly checking its remaining parser-integration gaps and known defects.

**#165 is a useful, narrowly scoped CLI improvement; #150 is the more complete MCP-1 implementation. Neither is ready unchanged.** Unlike the DATA-6 comparison, #165’s smaller approach fits the issue’s requirement to reuse MCP-2 contracts—it simply leaves much of MCP-1 unfinished.

MCP-1 directly links **#150 and #165**. #149/#166 address the related MCP-3 client-profile work rather than competing implementations of this issue.

| Dimension | #165 — `9a2a741` | #150 — `e0cd125` |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | CLI credentials, explicit manifests, report-size option | Remote authentication helpers, hosted OAuth regression cases, layered reports, external-server fixture |
| Base | `MCP-2` | `dev` |
| Architecture | Thin integration with existing production session and conformance APIs | Broader testing layer, also reusing existing primitives |
| OAuth regression coverage | Inherits existing tests; adds no independent registration/request regression matrix | Explicitly attempts that matrix, but its fixture builder couples some inputs |
| External-consumer evidence | No new external fixture or release-gate integration | Adds an external-server example and release-gate execution |
| New tests | One credential-validation test | Substantially broader lifecycle, OAuth, CLI, and external-server coverage |
| Verification | No dedicated build/test release check shown on the PR; author reports limited checks | McpFn release gate passes; SonarCloud fails |
| Overall | **Good-sized integration patch, insufficient issue coverage** | **Stronger completion candidate, with correctness defects** |

**The main problems in #165 are:**

1. **P1 — API keys can follow cross-origin redirects.**  
   `inspect` and `test-target` pass credentials through ordinary request headers without restricting redirects. I verified the forwarding path and reproduced Node forwarding a dummy `x-api-key` between two local origins. The authenticated conformance proxy’s restrictions do not protect these commands. [Credential injection](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/9a2a74153a9a1aa73a8907608821c758d1ca62d0/mcpfn/cli/src/index.ts#L316)

2. **P2 — Empty credential options silently disable authentication.**  
   An explicitly empty `--api-key-env` or `--bearer-token-env` is treated as absent. I reproduced the helper returning no headers. Invalid auth configuration should fail explicitly. [Validation](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/9a2a74153a9a1aa73a8907608821c758d1ca62d0/mcpfn/cli/src/index.ts#L341)

3. **Failure artifacts remain incomplete.**  
   The inherited suite throws on connection or manifest-check failures before constructing its report. The CLI prints the error, but does not write the requested machine-readable failure artifact. That falls short of MCP-1’s diagnostic requirements. [Suite execution](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/9a2a74153a9a1aa73a8907608821c758d1ca62d0/mcpfn/testing/src/suite.ts#L76)

**#150’s previously confirmed defects also remain:** failed connection/cleanup can skip credential disposal or revocation; registration and authorization-request client IDs are coupled; report annotation loses structured failure-phase information. Its header-based remote helper also warrants the same redirect protection.

**Recommendation:** use **#150’s broader regression and external-consumer coverage as the completion foundation**, adapted to MCP-2’s canonical contracts, and incorporate #165’s useful CLI options after fixing credential handling. Don’t treat #165’s smaller diff or green review checks as evidence that it completes MCP-1.

This assessment used the issue and delivery plan, current PR heads/checks, source inspection, and focused probes. I did not run either full release gate locally.
what did #165 miss and what question can I ask the agent which implement #165 to understand why it did that way

content.text:
**#149 is the stronger foundation for completing MCP-3. #166 is simpler and has better current build evidence, but its compatibility suite misses—and sometimes falsely passes—the failures this issue specifically wants to detect.**

Reviewed heads: #149 `44dc18b`; #166 `4b6dc85`.

MCP-3 requires more than profile hooks: it requires trustworthy evidence that projected catalogs, trusted argument enrichment, validation, and handler execution agree. [MCP-3 requirements](https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-3/add-deterministic-client-profile-contracts-and-actionable-schema)

| Dimension | #149 | #166 |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime lifecycle | Shared profile resolution, projection, call preparation, lifecycle diagnostics | Hooks integrated into real `tools/list` and `tools/call` |
| Trusted arguments | Explicit helper overwrites model-supplied values and rejects missing trusted context | Consumer implements that policy inside enrichment hook |
| Profile versions | Required versions and mismatch detection | Optional version labels; no corresponding mismatch enforcement |
| Catalog compatibility | Effective catalogs, change records, semantic diffs, symmetry analysis | Catalog hashes and optional snapshot comparison |
| Negative fixtures | Expectations for error code, stage, rejected property, and schema paths | Only `expectError: boolean` |
| Reporting | Richer evidence, but truncation and reachability defects | Smaller reports, but loses diagnostics and can report false success |
| CI | McpFn release gate fails | McpFn release gate passes; JavaScript failure is in unrelated UIFN tests |
| Overall | **Closer to the issue; needs repairs** | **Useful runtime foundation; inadequate compatibility gate** |

**The most consequential defects in #166:**

1. **A broken connection can pass a negative test.**  
   An `expectError: true` fixture accepts any thrown exception. My focused probe threw “connection lost”; the report returned `ok: true`. That does not prove strict validation rejected the intended input. [Fixture evaluation](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4b6dc8582000ccbca54e9318f68330a6a6a8249c/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profile-contract.ts#L104)

2. **Normal structured validation errors become empty evidence.**  
   The runner passes `result.structuredContent` to a helper expecting a different nesting shape. I supplied the runtime’s standard error envelope with AJV details; the report recorded `error: {}`. This directly undermines MCP-3’s requirement to preserve the rejected property and validation paths. [Error extraction](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4b6dc8582000ccbca54e9318f68330a6a6a8249c/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profile-contract.ts#L154)

3. **Connection failures can discard the entire report.**  
   Target creation and connection happen outside the error-handling block. A failure rejects the run instead of producing per-profile evidence. I reproduced this as well. [Connection setup](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4b6dc8582000ccbca54e9318f68330a6a6a8249c/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profile-contract.ts#L69)

**#149 is not ready either.** Its previously confirmed problems remain: silent truncation of evidence arrays, an unreliable `handlerReached: false` assertion, incomplete schema-portability traversal, and a TypeScript failure in the testing code. Its richer assertions are a better design, but their implementation needs correction.

**Recommendation:** finish #149’s broader contract and repair its evidence integrity. Consider #166’s smaller hooks and reuse of shared redaction utilities during that work. Do not replace #149 with #166 merely because #166 passes the dedicated release gate: its suite currently demonstrates false confidence in exactly the negative scenarios MCP-3 targets.

Verification included current source and CI inspection plus isolated exact-source probes with mocked clients. I did not run the full suites locally.

content.text:
**#168 is another small CLI-authentication patch, not a more complete MCP-1 solution. Compared with #165, it offers more flexible headers but weaker credential handling and fewer testing options. #150 remains the broadest implementation.**

Reviewed #168 at `0e5b9a0`; #150 and #165 remain at their previously reviewed heads.

| Dimension | #150 | #165 | #168 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main contribution | Regression harness, OAuth cases, reports, external fixture | Environment-backed CLI credentials | Arbitrary repeatable CLI headers |
| Credential input | Programmatic providers/header maps | Secret values read from environment | Secret values supplied in command arguments |
| Authenticated conformance | Harness support | Reuses loopback proxy | Reuses loopback proxy |
| CLI manifest verification | Broader harness work | Explicit `--manifest` | No equivalent option added |
| Configurable report cap | Reporting work | `--max-report-bytes` | No equivalent option added |
| New verification | Broad regression and consumer tests | Credential-parser test | Header-parser test |
| MCP-1 completeness | Closest, with known defects | Partial | Partial |

**The important findings in #168:**

1. **P1 — Custom credentials still follow cross-origin redirects.**  
   Like #165, authenticated `inspect` and `test-target` pass headers directly to the SDK without redirect restrictions. The previously reproduced API-key forwarding behavior applies to this unchanged transport path. The conformance proxy’s protection does not cover these commands. [HTTP target creation](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/0e5b9a06c877a7ae4eb2d5bf0f8f7e9c4ba42f79/mcpfn/cli/src/index.ts#L297)

2. **Credential handling is weaker than #165’s.**  
   `--header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"` expands the token into process arguments. Excluding headers from reports does not prevent that exposure. #165’s environment-variable-name approach avoids putting the value in argv.

3. **P2 — Documented authentication examples send literal variable names.**  
   The README uses single quotes around `'Authorization: Bearer $MCP_TOKEN'` and `'X-API-Key: $MCP_TEST_KEY'`. The shell does not expand those variables, and the parser does not resolve them. These examples send placeholder text instead of credentials. [README examples](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/0e5b9a06c877a7ae4eb2d5bf0f8f7e9c4ba42f79/mcpfn/cli/README.md#L11)

4. **It leaves the earlier completeness gaps unresolved.**  
   No new independent OAuth registration/request matrix, external-consumer regression fixture, or structured connection-failure reporting. Its inherited suite can still throw before producing the requested report.

The implementation itself is compact and readable. However, the added test exercises header parsing—not actual credential delivery, redirect containment, authenticated conformance, or failure artifacts. The reported **11 tests are the CLI suite total**, not 11 new authentication tests. The dedicated McpFn release checks were still running when inspected.

**Recommendation:** retain #150 as the broader completion foundation. For the CLI addition, prefer #165’s environment-backed credential design, potentially extended with #168’s multiple-header flexibility through secret-safe configuration. **#168 does not supersede #165 on quality or either PR on MCP-1 coverage.**

This was a read-only source comparison with focused parser probes; I did not rerun the full release gate.

Reading the issue and its architecture plan changed the recommendation: the central requirement is a canonical protocol representation and structural extraction that cannot drift from it. ## Requirements and sources [DATA-6 issue](https://linear.app/21n/issue/DATA-6/expose-canonical-structural-resource-selector-extraction) [Architecture and Delivery Plan](https://linear.app/21n/document/data-6-architecture-and-delivery-plan-8556ea15ae1f) [Ideation and Product Rationale](https://linear.app/21n/document/data-6-ideation-and-product-rationale-acd52cdf6e65) The helper must identify resource selectors in supported protocol positions, including batch/transaction envelopes, without recursively treating arbitrary application data as selectors. For example, a request targeting tasks can contain a record whose resource field says secret-documents; that nested application value is not itself a protocol selector. The plan calls for a versioned parsed representation, typed normalized selectors, explicit malformed/version errors, and parser/extractor conformance fixtures. Extraction is a structural visitor over parsed protocol data. Application validation belongs in parsing/validation; product-specific authorization and tenant placement stay outside the helper. Downstream migration should demonstrate removal of local recursive traversal. ## Reviewed snapshots
PRHeadApproach
[#153](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/153)4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43feaCore versioned parser, discriminated union, separate collector, server reexports and documentation; about 20 files
[#164](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/164)8da10bf3f3d205e33331b9283251c0fed9f7b5caServer-side action plus unknown payload switch, application-schema lookup and extraction; 4 files
Both were based on dev. This is a September 2026 review snapshot, not a fresh check of current heads. Harness/model attribution is not established here; the user-supplied MCP-1 mappings must not be transferred to these PRs. ## The problem and two solutions, simply #153 first translates a request into a recognized official form, then reads the resource fields from that form. When protocol variants change, the parser types and visitor can be checked together. #164 looks at the raw request and follows its own checklist of where resource fields should be. That is better than searching every nested object, but it creates another place that needs updating whenever the protocol changes. The distinction is not that a large refactor is automatically better. It is whether the server and extractor share the same definition of request structure. #153 moves toward that design; #164 maintains parallel knowledge. #153 still needs stronger proof that actual execution routes consume the shared representation or an equivalent common schema. ## Comparison

## #153 findings and limits - **Authorization example is unsafe for selectorless broad requests.** The documentation uses selectors.every(allowed), which returns true for an empty list. An omitted search/clone/pull selector can have broad execution meaning. The example needs explicit policy for that case. Returning an empty structural set is not inherently wrong: the issue leaves selectorless semantics open. - **Reserved actor-feed cursor becomes a resource.** Pull extraction includes __datafn_actor_feed__ among resource selectors, which can make an ordinary resource allowlist reject normal synchronization. - **Batch version validation gap.** The parser bypasses explicit protocolVersion validation for array payloads. - Shared action names alone do not prove canonical route parsing. Query auth integration is useful, but is not complete conformance evidence for every operation. - No evidence was established that the downstream Skillplane integration removed its local traversal and exercised the canonical helper. [Authorization example](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/docs/content/docs/documentation/security/resource-selectors.mdx#L87) [Pull cursor handling](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/core/src/protocol.ts#L439) [Batch parsing](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/4eb55d039f969a4b37913aacf88fc85285c43fea/datafn/core/src/protocol.ts#L550) ## #164 findings and limits - **P2: status route incompatibility.** The extractor requires an object payload even for status, but GET status reaches the authorization wrapper with null. An exact-source probe returned DFQL_INVALID instead of the expected selectorless result. - **P2: REST request incompatibility.** GET query has a null body, and POST REST query can omit body.resource because the resource comes from the URL. Authorization runs before the REST route derives that selector. The helper lacks that route input and rejects these valid request shapes. - The outer envelope is not a parsed protocol union. Its own switch can diverge from route validators; schema membership checks do not solve structural drift. - Full-schema expansion mixes execution/authorization policy into structural extraction. It can be conservative, but it is a different contract and must be explicit. - Passing a null envelope causes a native TypeError. This is a lower-priority robustness concern because typed callers violate the declared contract. - **Rejected concern:** empty search resources were checked against provider and native execution; they produced no results. This was not established as an authorization bypass. - **Scope correction:** indirectly related resources are not automatically missing selectors. The requirement is structural extraction, not discovery of every resource execution might subsequently touch. It proposed a versioned union, shared route/execution parsing, an exhaustive visitor, and parser/extractor fixtures. That explanation agrees with the key architectural criticism. It does not mean every operation validator must be rewritten. The smallest sound change can share structural parsing or schemas while retaining operation-specific validation. ## Recommended completion Use #153's separation as the foundation. Fix actor-feed filtering, version handling and the selectorless authorization example. Establish one shared source of protocol structure with real route/execution coverage, including REST and status. Add conformance fixtures for each supported envelope and demonstrate the downstream helper replacement. ## Question for the implementing agent The issue documents ask for selector extraction from a canonical parsed protocol representation, sharing protocol structure with the server. Why did you instead build a separate action-based switch over unknown payloads? What prevents it from drifting when routes or envelopes change? **Preferred foundation: #170, 7/10, Needs fixes.** Compared with #150 (6.5/10), #165 (5/10) and #168 (4/10), #170 addresses the broadest useful portion of MCP-1 and fixes important credential/lifecycle shortcomings. Its regression assertions still produce false passes, so it is not merge-ready.

[PR #170](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/170), reviewed head \`f796d70a86a0c71787472f437ba182a2e7c04af8\`, base \`dev\`, 35 changed files. Source reads and probes used its existing worktree; only .conduct records were dirty. HEAD and tracked source cleanliness were rechecked after tests; no implementation files were edited.

### Harness, model and independence
Codex Desktop, **gpt-5.6-sol**, confirmed in local thread metadata and every available turn_context. Session \`01a08bb0-f9fe-7951-aed1-965679939fc3\` is the previously unscored new Sol run. User explicitly requested ignoring existing MCP-1 PRs/worktrees. The visible transcript states it complied; this differs from Devin's review-informed planning samples. No assumption is made that the current Linear delegate created the PR.

### Confirmed findings
1. **P1 — Ordinary execution errors are reported as successful hosted authorization.** [host-authorization.ts:315](${base}mcpfn/testing/src/host-authorization.ts#L315). The catch path passes an error message without an OAuth code; outcome is derived only from errorCode, so a normal Error becomes allowed. Reproduced with prepareRegistration throwing “registration unavailable”: ChatGPT, Claude and DCR positive cases all returned status passed at client-registration, with that error attached. Execution failure must fail independently of expected OAuth rejection semantics.
2. **P1 — A positive OAuth case can pass without completed authorization or usable tokens.** [host-authorization.ts:254](${base}mcpfn/testing/src/host-authorization.ts#L254), [token validation:271](${base}mcpfn/testing/src/host-authorization.ts#L271). A 200 login response is accepted; missing callback code is replaced with fixture.token.code or literal “code”. Token responses need no access_token/token_type; refresh success checks only HTTP success. Reproduced with GET returning “login not completed” and all POSTs returning only a dummy refresh_token: all three positive cases passed. This is separate from finding 1: no exception is thrown. Require a validated callback/code/state, valid token responses and authenticated resource/MCP evidence before claiming a completed flow.
3. **P2 — JUnit can show green for an incomplete JSON run.** [reports.ts:112](${base}mcpfn/testing/src/reports.ts#L112). A report with ok:false and dropped diagnostic events becomes one successful fallback testcase, failures=0 and artifact.truncated=false. Incomplete scenarios also emit failure elements without inclusion in the failures count. Reproduced with a structurally valid incomplete report. Represent all suite-level incompleteness as explicit failing/incomplete JUnit evidence and keep counts consistent.
4. **P2 — Explicit visible-tool expectations are ignored without a manifest.** [suite.ts:108](${base}mcpfn/testing/src/suite.ts#L108). expectedToolNames is consumed only inside the optional manifest branch. Reproduced against the actual SDK-only server with expectedToolNames=[“THIS_TOOL_DOES_NOT_EXIST”]: ok:true, manifestChecked:false. Validate the requested inventory independently or reject the unsupported option combination.

The existing GitHub review independently flags findings 1, 3 and 4. These are confirmed here by source inspection and probes, not merely copied review assertions. Finding 2 was additionally reproduced here.

### Strengths and remaining acceptance boundaries
- Delegates MCP transport/session work to the existing production client; reuses shared PKCE and OAuth redaction instead of creating another engine.
- Adds bounded credential headers, redirect:error, acquire/revoke/dispose ownership, concurrent-close memoization, and cleanup for rejected conformance setup. This materially improves the earlier implementations.
- Environment-backed CLI credentials avoid raw secrets in argv; missing/empty credentials are rejected. Connection failures now produce structured target reports. Pretty JSON cap calculation is corrected.
- Adds JSON/JUnit schema and package provenance, an SDK-only authenticated external fixture, packed export assertions, post-publication registry consumer checks and CI artifact upload.
- Hosted fixture inputs are separately represented and allow deliberate redirect drift. However the new matrix runs against an injected registration map and permissive token authority; it does not itself prove real DCR/metadata discovery, callback validation, code/verifier binding, or OAuth-derived MCP initialization. Passing its one positive matrix test is not proof of those boundaries.
- Registry verification is explicitly post-publication and has not yet proved installation of the new released versions. Full conformance/report failure semantics still need adversarial checks. The conformance CLI exposes JSON --report, while --junit is exposed on test-target; the PR description's statement that conformance also adds JUnit is broader than the implemented CLI.

### Verification evidence
Independently rerun under Node 22.22.0: testing package **9 files / 34 tests passed**; CLI **11 tests passed**; testing TypeScript passed; official-SDK-only external fixture passed **2 authenticated scenarios**, unauthenticated exit 1, JSON and JUnit output. Four targeted probes reproduced the findings above. The first testing invocation used the repository cwd and found no tests; rerunning from the package cwd produced the results reported here.

The implementation transcript and local completion record report **73 release-gate steps passed on the final code**, including packed consumers, Playwright and official conformance. That full gate was not rerun during this review. At the latest GitHub snapshot, McpFn Node 18 CJS and Sonar passed; McpFn release gate/JavaScript were still pending and four Python jobs failed. Those Python failures have not been diagnosed here and are not presented as changed-code defects. No live registry publication or downstream deployment is claimed.

### Where the agent went wrong
The agent improved scope ownership and verification persistence substantially: after the user corrected its unnecessary browser detour, it read Linear, implemented the broader contract, rebuilt the native dependency and reran the full gate after a cleanup fix. Its remaining mistake was treating happy-path fixture success and a green gate as proof that the harness recognizes broken behavior. The core outcome classifier ignores uncoded exceptions; permissive token mocks let fabricated codes and incomplete token responses look successful; reporters and CLI options lack cross-contract consistency tests. The completion statement still overclaims MCP-1 until these negative-path invariants are tested.

#170 **7/10** > #150 **6.5/10** > #165 **5/10** > #168 **4/10** for the reviewed snapshots. Use #170 as the next implementation foundation. These scores describe overall delivered usefulness and coverage; the P1 false positives remain merge blockers regardless of rank.

before proceeding suggest improvements in the Notion QA hub that we created - right now - it looks very messy with each page having too much info, no sturctured template for analysis pages, score card being present in same database, no overview table in each page on the top with summary for each combination etc

I’d restructure it around **three layers: a dashboard, issue comparisons, and individual implementation reviews**. The detailed evidence stays available without dominating the pages you read.

**1. Make the QA Hub a dashboard**

Move the scorecard out of the issue database into its own page. The hub should contain:

- **Harness and model scorecard** — current ratings, sample sizes, confidence, and changes.
- **Issue comparisons** — one row per Linear issue.
- **Implementation reviews** — one row per PR or cloud session.
- **Review queue** — implementations awaiting review, plus reviewed PRs with newer commits.

This separates “which issue?”, “which implementation?”, and “what have we learned overall?”

**2. Give every issue page the same compact template**

Start with a short conclusion, then an overview table:

| Implementation | Harness | Model | Score | Verdict | Main strength | Main blocker |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| #170 | Codex Desktop | Sol | 7 | Needs fixes | Broad coverage | Auth false positives |
| #150 | Cursor | Grok 4.6 | 6.5 | Needs fixes | Strong foundation | Credential cleanup |
| #165 | Tembo | Sol | 5 | Partial | Environment-backed secrets | Missing issue scope |
| #168 | Codex Desktop | Terra | 4 | Partial | Working CLI increment | Narrow delivery |

Below that, use this fixed order:

1. **What the issue requires** — five to eight acceptance criteria.
2. **Acceptance coverage matrix** — implementations as columns; criteria as rows.
3. **Recommendation** — preferred foundation and why.
4. **Key differences** — only findings that materially distinguish implementations.
5. **Linked implementation reviews** — detailed findings and evidence.
6. **Decision history** — collapsed, dated changes to the recommendation.

Keep this page focused on comparison. Don’t repeat full PR descriptions, transcripts, or every test result.

**3. Give each PR/session its own implementation review**

Use a consistent template:

- **Summary:** score, verdict, harness, model, reviewed commit, review date.
- **Assessment:** scope coverage, architecture, correctness, verification, reporting accuracy.
- **Findings:** severity, problem, consequence, evidence, status.
- **Validation:** independently reproduced versus agent-reported versus unavailable.
- **Agent behavior:** consequential decisions, missed requirements, response to feedback.
- **Evidence:** links to transcript and supporting artifacts.
- **Revision history:** what changed between reviewed commits.

Put full transcripts in **child evidence pages**, with a short summary and relevant excerpts in the review.

**4. Separate fields that currently get conflated**

Use distinct properties for:

| Property | Examples |
|---|---|
| Review status | Not reviewed, In review, Reviewed, Re-review needed |
| Implementation scope | Complete, Partial, Planning only |
| Verdict | Ready, Needs fixes, Not assessed |
| Attribution confidence | Execution metadata, Provider badge, User supplied, Unknown |
| Validation confidence | Reproduced, Source inspected, Agent reported |
| Review freshness | Current head, New commits since review |

This would make #169 visibly **“Not reviewed”**, rather than leaving its exclusion buried in prose.

**5. Make the scorecard explain the evidence behind ratings**

Show **harness–model combinations first**, then cautious aggregate summaries. Each score should include:

- Reviewed PR count **and distinct issue count**
- Planning versus implementation
- Independent work versus reused implementations
- Latest review date
- A link to the contributing reviews

That makes “Desktop + Sol: 7 on one issue” easier to interpret than a single Desktop average mixing Sol and Terra.

**My recommendation:** keep the current database as **Issue Comparisons**, create **Implementation Reviews**, and move the scorecard to the hub. Preserve existing content as linked evidence/history while replacing the main pages with the consistent templates above.

const r=await tools.mcp__codex_apps__notion_notion_create_pages({parent:{page_id:load("hub").id},pages:[{properties:{title:"Review guide & reusable templates"},content:`## Working rules - Create one Issue Comparison per Linear issue and one Implementation Review per PR or session; link them with the Issue relation. - Keep the issue overview concise. Put full transcripts and historical analysis in evidence child pages. - Record the reviewed commit separately from the captured head. New commits change Review Status to Re-review needed; an existing score remains historical. - Never convert Not reviewed into Needs fixes or Ready. Scope, review status and quality verdict answer different questions. - Record model evidence precisely: execution metadata, provider badge, user-supplied attribution, requested model, or unknown. A composer label does not prove historical execution. - Separate independent reproduction, source inspection and agent claims. A green gate is not proof that negative cases fail. - Planning ratings stay separate from implementation scores. Record reused implementation and access to prior reviews. - Scores: 10 complete/safe/verified; 7 strong foundation with important fixes; 5 useful work with substantial gaps; 3 narrow/unreliable deliverable. Do not manufacture scores to fill blank cells. - Linked queue views update from properties. GitHub freshness and narrative comparison tables require updating when a new review or head is captured; no background monitor is configured. ## Issue comparison template Duplicate an existing issue page's structure or copy these sections; use the native table pattern already present on each page. 1. Overview table: Implementation | Harness/model | Score | Review/verdict | Strength | Main gap. 2. Recommendation: preferred foundation, reason, and important review exclusions. 3. What the issue requires: source issue and 5–8 acceptance criteria. 4. Acceptance coverage table: criteria as rows, implementations as columns; distinguish demonstrated, gap, author claim, and unreviewed. 5. Key differences: only consequential distinctions. 6. Detailed implementation review links. 7. Evidence child page and collapsed decision history. ## Implementation review template 1. Summary table: implementation, harness/model, score, review status, verdict. 2. Assessment: scope, architecture, correctness, verification, reporting/process. 3. Findings: severity, triggering behavior, consequence, source/probe and current status. 4. Validation: independent results, author-reported results and unavailable checks. 5. Agent behavior: consequential decisions and missed requirements. 6. Evidence: PR/session, issue relation, transcript, reviewed SHA, captured SHA and freshness. 7. Collapsed revision history: changes in findings, evidence and score. ## Evidence template Record the issue/PR/session, capture date and source. Preserve original messages and review snapshots with their timestamps. Label omissions or unavailable transcripts. Keep historical findings attached to historical commits. Link back to the current review and avoid silently rewriting original evidence. ## Update checklist - [ ] Read the issue and applicable decisions. - [ ] Capture PR head and model attribution. - [ ] Review code and meaningful failure cases. - [ ] Record tests and limitations. - [ ] Update findings, status, verdict and commit freshness. - [ ] Refresh issue overview and acceptance matrix. - [ ] Update scorecard sample counts and revision note only if justified. `}],allow_async:false});const p=JSON.parse(r.content[0].text).pages[0];store("guide",p);text(p); const score=load("reorg-rows").find(x=>x.Issue==="Cross-issue"); await tools.mcp__codex_apps__notion_fetch({id:score.id}); const tbl=rs=>' '+rs.map(r=>""+r.map(x=>``).join("")+"").join(" ")+"

Reviewed 2026-09-11. Head `a6592039ede06554a56de8c12044ab24e4c9a0ed`, rechecked unchanged at completion. [PR](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/171). Codex Desktop / GPT-5.6 Sol, verified from local execution metadata. **7.5/10 — Needs fixes. Preferred MCP-3 foundation.**

## Comparison

| Implementation | Assessment | Relative result |
|---|---|---|
| #171 / Codex Desktop / Sol | 7.5/10; shared runtime lifecycle, explicit ownership, full catalog hashes, dialect-aware portability, CLI and stronger gates | New preferred foundation; three remaining evidence/diagnostic defects |
| #149 / Cursor / model unverified | Earlier qualitative review; broad contracts but changed-code type error and false assertions | Previously preferred; now superseded by #171 |
| #166 / Tembo / Sol | Earlier qualitative review; compact hooks but transport errors could satisfy negative scenarios | Weaker correctness and scope |
| #169 / Codex Desktop / Terra | Earlier 4/10; null projection exposed hidden tools and thin compatibility suite falsely passed | Substantially weaker |

Earlier PR assessments are retained from the prior review, not rerun at their current heads in this batch. No individual numeric score is invented for #149/#166. This comparison is not a controlled model benchmark.

## Requirements and architecture

Read the current [Linear issue](https://linear.app/21n/issue/MCP-3/add-deterministic-client-profile-contracts-and-actionable-schema) and [Architecture & Delivery Plan](https://linear.app/21n/document/architecture-and-delivery-plan-mcp-3-add-deterministic-client-profile-3a4491491f7a) through Linear MCP. MCP-3 requires authenticated profile selection, list/call symmetry, trusted enrichment before canonical validation, handler reachability evidence, exact structural errors, portable schemas, snapshots, and redacted bounded reports.

#171 substantially implements the intended runtime/testing/CLI split. Verified identity drives matching; self-reported metadata is separate. Hidden tools are rejected on calls, forged server-owned values are rejected, enrichers cannot alter model-owned properties, no-profile listing preserves its old path, and unsafe fixtures are explicitly incomplete. Full tool hashes detect schema changes. Real AJV dialect validators replace the shallow object checks of #169. Reports expose truncation, targets run serially and connect failures remain failures.

## Findings

### P2 — Negative fixtures do not prove that execution stopped before the handler

[client-profile-contracts.ts:469](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/a6592039ede06554a56de8c12044ab24e4c9a0ed/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profile-contracts.ts#L469)

The suite treats error.details.lifecycleStage in the tool result as evidence of execution phase. It has no handler-reachability assertion or trusted lifecycle receipt. A handler can return a domain error with the same input-validation envelope after execution, and the negative contract passes. This matters when validation moves from canonical validation into a handler or a returned domain error: the test no longer proves the promised pre-side-effect boundary.

Reproduced using the real server, target and in-memory MCP transport: allow the unknown property through the canonical schema, increment a handler counter, then return MCPFN_INVALID_ARGUMENTS with input-validation details and the expected rejected property. Report: ok=true; handler calls=1. The probe uses an intentionally misleading returned domain envelope to test whether the suite independently verifies its claim. It does not show that normal core validation invokes the handler on invalid input.

Fix: bind expected stage/handlerReached to trusted runtime observations for in-process targets and an explicit authenticated evidence adapter for remote targets; mark unavailable evidence incomplete rather than equating payload assertions with execution proof.

### P2 — Ordinary thrown errors lose lifecycle details

[server.ts:437](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/a6592039ede06554a56de8c12044ab24e4c9a0ed/mcpfn/core/src/server.ts#L437)

Only McpFnError instances are wrapped with lifecycleStage and profile. A normal Error from a handler or enricher passes straight to errorResult, losing that information. The optional evidence sink receives a stage, but the compatibility runner cannot consume that sink for a remote target. A fixture expecting handler-stage failure therefore fails despite the known runtime stage.

Reproduced: handler throws new Error('ordinary failure'); result has MCPFN_TOOL_ERROR but no lifecycleStage; the suite fails with 'Expected lifecycle stage handler'. The existing stage test throws McpFnValidationError, so it misses ordinary exceptions.

Fix: normalize all caught error forms into the structured lifecycle envelope while preserving domain codes and safe details.

### P2 — Error-code mismatch bypasses report redaction

[client-profile-contracts.ts:462](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/a6592039ede06554a56de8c12044ab24e4c9a0ed/mcpfn/testing/src/client-profile-contracts.ts#L462)

The error-code mismatch branch interpolates the received code directly, and that string is stored in the report without boundedError/redactOAuthValue. Codes returned by arbitrary targets are not guaranteed safe strings. This bypass is distinct from the redacted exception path.

Reproduced: a tool returns a code derived from fixture input `token=private-customer-argument-7391`; the expectation is EXPECTED. The final JSON report retains the full token string. No real secret was used. Fixture values are normally excluded, but reflected values can re-enter through this unchecked path.

Fix: use fixed mismatch messages or sanitize/validate both codes before including them, then apply report-wide redaction as defense in depth.

## Validation

- 72 core + 30 testing + 11 CLI existing tests passed locally (113 total).
- Three additional reviewer probes reproduced the three findings. A passing reproduction asserts observed faulty behavior, not correctness.
- Core, testing and CLI TypeScript checks passed against the exact source snapshot, with built workspace dependencies from the same PR head.

- No source changes, fixes, PR comments, pushes or merges were made. Review probes exist only in temporary detached snapshots.

Local session `01a08c0a-3148-7441-bb72-1c0e1b14e608` consistently records gpt-5.6-sol. User explicitly told it to use Linear and ignore existing PRs/worktrees. This is an inference from code/tests, not a claim about hidden reasoning. See agent-transcript.md for the user/assistant transcript.

content.text:
These are from the **last review snapshot**, not a new review. The fixes below are proposed and haven’t been applied. :codex-annotation{index="1"}

**[#170 — MCP-1](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/170): credential handling and trustworthy reports**

- **Failed credential cleanup becomes impossible to retry.** When the server disconnects or connection opening is aborted, the client can discard its connection handle even though credential revocation/disposal failed. Later `close()` calls cannot finish cleanup, and diagnostics can incorrectly say it succeeded.  
  **Fix:** retain ownership of the handle until cleanup succeeds; allow subsequent cleanup attempts and report failures accurately. Test remote disconnects and aborted connections with a provider that fails once, then succeeds.

- **Credentials can leak through object keys.** Redaction preserves keys to avoid damaging report structure. But server-controlled metadata could contain `{ "<credential>": "value" }`, exposing the credential in inspector output.  
  **Fix:** distinguish trusted report fields from server-controlled data. Preserve the former; redact both keys and values in the latter.

- **Redaction can corrupt results.** If a credential happens to be `"passed"`, redaction can replace the legitimate test status with `"[REDACTED]"`. JSON then reports success while JUnit interprets the result as failure.  
  **Fix:** preserve trusted status values while scrubbing untrusted content. Verify JSON/JUnit agreement with deliberately colliding credentials.

- **The report limit applies too late.** Redaction traverses effectively unlimited input before enforcing the output-size cap. Deep or enormous server responses can exhaust memory or the stack.  
  **Fix:** enforce traversal limits during redaction and explicitly mark reports incomplete when limits are reached. Simply restoring arbitrary truncation risks silently damaging report structure.

There is also a small missing positive test for lowercase `application/json`. The cleanup and redaction defects are the substantive blockers.

**[#155 — UIF-2](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/155): generated projects and popup behavior**

- **Popups can disappear or render in the wrong document.** A root document without a `<body>` gets no portal content. An iframe popup with `container={null}` can instead render in the parent document.  
  **Fix:** treat `null` and `undefined` consistently; resolve the root’s owner document and use its `body`, falling back to `documentElement`. Preserve explicit container targets.

- **Menu presets change the wrong styling.** `menuTreatment` modifies an overlay-shadow variable used by dialogs, while menus use a different variable. Menus remain unchanged and dialogs unexpectedly lose shadows.  
  **Fix:** emit menu-specific styling and test that changing menu treatment leaves dialog styling intact.

- **Generated projects omit necessary dependencies.** Selecting Heroicons or Phosphor records the choice but doesn’t install its package. React scaffolds also omit `@types/react` and `@types/react-dom`.  
  **Fix:** include the selected icon package and React declarations in generated manifests; verify generated projects can typecheck and build.

- **Its own CI build fails.** `@uifn/create` reports React component-type incompatibilities in preview code and tests.  
  **Fix:** reproduce the CI dependency/type resolution, reconcile the React type contracts, and rebuild. The precise cause still needs investigation; suppressing errors with casts would not establish correctness.

**[#153 — DATA-6](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/153): correct authorization inputs**

- **Internal join-store cursors are reported as application resources.** Ordinary sync requests include generated `join_*` cursor keys. The extractor returns those as resources, so a gateway can reject a valid request unless someone incorrectly grants access to internal storage names.  
  **Fix:** explicitly distinguish internal cursor identifiers from resource selectors. Either exclude them where authorization is already covered or map them to their endpoint resources using trusted metadata. Avoid a blanket prefix filter that could hide legitimate resources.

- **Malformed REST resources reach authorization callbacks.** Preflight decodes the resource segment but doesn’t apply the handler’s full validation. A value such as `../etc` can reach authorization before the handler rejects it. This finding does **not** establish successful filesystem traversal.  
  **Fix:** share one segment validator and run it before selector extraction and authorization. Test that malformed segments never invoke authorization callbacks.

- **It now conflicts with `dev` in two documentation files.**  
  **Fix:** integrate the merged DataFn changes, preserve both documentation additions, and rerun parser/extractor and authorization regressions.

**[#133 — DocsFn](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/pull/133): several independent edge cases**

| Problem | Potential fix |
|---|---|
| Generated JSON imports use syntax unsupported by older versions within its declared Node range | Generate compatible modules, or deliberately raise and test the minimum Node version |
| Version switchers navigate to nonexistent page versions, producing 404s | When explicit version links are supplied, disable unavailable versions instead of inventing URLs; fix React and Svelte |
| Duplicate tab values produce ambiguous React behavior and Svelte duplicate-key errors | Reject duplicates during compilation with an actionable error |
| Route configuration accepts `//example.com`, creating external links | Require local paths with a single leading slash; reject query/fragment syntax and other URL-escape forms |
| Accepted OpenAPI 3.2 documents lose local reference descriptions | Apply the supported override behavior consistently across accepted versions; add a 3.2 regression |
| A config-loading test timed out in CI | Reproduce under CI-like conditions and establish whether loading is slow or the test is flaky before changing timeouts |

There is also a minor misleading HTML-comment test name. Separately, its obsolete **Docs Guardrails** failure should be addressed by integrating the already-merged #167; that is distinct from the config-test timeout.

My recommended fix order is **#170 → #153 → #155 → #133**: credential/report integrity first, authorization inputs next, then scaffold correctness and the broader DocsFn work.
